name: Gender-neutral aesthetics / 'pretty boy' / softboy

lead: This aesthetic aims for soft, delicate, androgynous features in men instead of heavy masculine angularity.
People pursue it with skincare, hair, grooming, makeup and clothing.

paras: Followers emphasize smooth skin, eyes, lips and styled hair, and choose clothing and grooming that read as soft and polished.
Mostly styling choices; any procedures people pair with it carry their own risks.

chain: Prioritize skin, hair, eyes and grooming
angle.text: Followers of the look use skincare, haircare, grooming, makeup and styling to emphasize smooth skin and delicate features. It is a styling and grooming approach rather than a single product.

lead: Gender-neutral, 'pretty boy' or softboy aesthetics describe a look built on soft, delicate or androgynous features in men: smooth skin, defined eyes and lips, a gentler jawline and often groomed hair, rather than heavy, angular dimorphism. People pursue it through skincare, hair, grooming, makeup, fashion and sometimes facial procedures.[1]

The look has long precedent in popular culture, from 1970s glam figures such as David Bowie and Marc Bolan to Prince and Boy George, and Japanese and Korean pop culture has treated androgynous looks as a positive attribute.[1]
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as an alternative target to the 'chad' ideal: instead of maximizing masculine bone structure, users optimize skin, eyes, hair and harmony.

paras: The aesthetic emphasizes softness: clear skin, expressive eyes, fuller lips, styled hair and a less pronounced jaw. Practitioners adapt fashion and grooming to match, including jewelry, makeup and unisex clothing, which became mainstream in men's fashion in the West and Asia.[1]

Androgynous fashion appears across the twentieth century, from 1920s flappers and Marlene Dietrich to Yves Saint Laurent's 1966 tuxedo suit, Bowie's Ziggy Stardust in 1972, and 1980s figures such as Prince and Boy George.[1]

timeline.event: David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona becomes a symbol of sexual ambiguity.[1]
Yves Saint Laurent introduces the women's tuxedo suit Le Smoking.[1]
